classification.difficultyReason: Development: compare category frequencies within and across two classes, then explain why numerical distribution language does not apply to vegetable categories. Part d requires transferring the explicitly taught distinction between numerical positions and categorical spacing to this back-to-back display.

inlines.text: A back-to-back dot plot can be used to compare two data sets.
7A and 7B were surveyed about their favourite vegetable.

spec.description: Three-column categorical display. Class 7A dots extend left from the centre; Class 7B dots extend right. One header rule and two vertical dividers; no axes or numeric ticks.
spec.mathematics: Rows Carrots, Peas, Potato, Broccoli, Snow peas, Pumpkin. Class 7A counts 10,0,6,5,3,2. Class 7B counts 4,6,11,5,0,1.
spec.answerVisibility: All category labels and dots are permanent supplied question data.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Which vegetable is most popular in 7A?

answer.worked: Carrots have the most dots in Class 7A: $10$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Which vegetable is most popular in class 7B?

answer.worked: Potato has the most dots in Class 7B: $11$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Which vegetable is the most popular overall?

answer.worked:
Combine the counts from both classes.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Carrots}&=10+4=14\\\text{Peas}&=0+6=6\\\text{Potato}&=6+11=17\\\text{Broccoli}&=5+5=10\\\text{Snow peas}&=3+0=3\\\text{Pumpkin}&=2+1=3\end{align*}$$
Potato has the greatest total, $17$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Explain why it wouldn’t make sense to talk about outliers, clustering, gaps for this data set.

answer.short: The data is categorical; vegetable names have no numerical order or meaningful numerical distances.
answer.worked: Vegetable names are categories, rather than positions on a numerical scale. Their order can change, so separation between categories does not represent numerical gaps, clusters or outliers.
